top_choice_rationale: P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is the sharpest case on the slate of a clear question paired with a transparent, reusable design. The China-shock papers show how import competition reaches local labour markets, and they contradicted the expectation of fast, frictionless reallocation. The finding of slow and costly adjustment has survived repeated re-analysis, including critiques of shift-share inference. Attribution is tight, because the three are co-authors of the central papers and Dorn is a co-originator. The citation is narrowed to empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment. It leaves out the skill-premium work and the task-model theory that sit with Katz, Goldin, Acemoglu and Restrepo. The costs are that the technology and trade strands could be read as two discoveries, that Katz is omitted, and that the size and persistence of the local effects are still debated. I rely on background recall, not verified citation data. I rank P001 (Kiyotaki-Moore) second because it is a mature mechanism with the cleanest attribution, although direct identification of the collateral channel is mixed. P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is third. It is a strong, validated method, but the three-name cap forces a visible omission, Pakes' share is larger than the others', and the counterfactuals depend on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions. I rank no award last because all three proposals describe mature, attributable achievements.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. None of my listed co-authors or affiliations (Johannesson, Ellingsen, Brodeur, Camerer, Rand, Nowak, Fudenberg, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Johan Almenberg) is a credited name on P001, P002 or P003. I disclose collegial SSE ties to committee members Andersson, Friberg and Strömberg, and a co-authorship with the former member Johannesson, without adjudicating them. My metascience orientation may lead me to weight transparent, re-analysable evidence more heavily than colleagues do.
